question: In a colon cancer screening program, a 52-year-old patient undergoes a colonoscopy. The entire colon is normal in appearance, except for the finding of a 2 cm pedicled sigmoid polyp that is removed with a diathermy loop. The anatomopathological result indicates that there is carcinoma "in situ" limited to the head of the polyp. He has a thoracoabdominal CT reported as normal. Indicate what would be the correct conduct to follow:

options.opa: Segmental resection of the affected colon.
options.opc: Local resection of the base of the polyp.

enhanced_information: In the case of a 52-year-old patient with a 2 cm pedicled sigmoid polyp showing carcinoma in situ confined to the head of the polyp, and a normal thoracoabdominal CT scan, the standard medical consensus is that the risk of metastasis is low. Carcinoma in situ indicates that the cancer has not invaded beyond the polyp, and the normal CT scan supports the absence of distant disease. Therefore, aggressive surgical interventions such as segmental resection, local resection of the polyp base, or sigmoidectomy with lymphadenectomy are unnecessary. The appropriate management is periodic endoscopic surveillance to monitor for any recurrence or new polyp formation. Thus, periodic endoscopic surveillance remains the best consensus-supported approach.
analysis: In this scenario, the patient has a 2 cm pedicled sigmoid polyp with carcinoma in situ confined to the head of the polyp. Carcinoma in situ is a non-invasive form of cancer, meaning it has not penetrated the basement membrane or spread beyond the polyp. The normal thoracoabdominal CT scan further supports the absence of metastatic disease. Given these findings, the risk of metastasis is low, and aggressive surgical interventions are not warranted. The standard medical practice for managing carcinoma in situ in a polyp, especially when it is completely excised and there is no evidence of invasion or metastasis, is to conduct periodic endoscopic surveillance. This approach allows for monitoring of any recurrence or the development of new polyps, while avoiding unnecessary surgical risks. Therefore, the most appropriate and consensus-supported management strategy is periodic endoscopic surveillance.
